Calculus · Part I · Functions, limits and continuity

Module 3Continuity and infinity

Learn what it means for a function to be continuous, and what continuity guarantees: solutions of equations, which the bisection method finds to any accuracy you ask for, and largest and smallest values. Then follow functions out to infinity, through asymptotes and limits at infinity, to the orders of growth behind big-O notation.

⏱ 270 minYou need: Modules 1 and 2

In this module you will

  • Decide whether a function is continuous at a point, and classify its discontinuities
  • Explain why the standard functions are continuous on their domains, and use continuity to find limits
  • Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that an equation has a solution, and find it by bisection to a guaranteed accuracy
  • State the Extreme Value Theorem, and show with examples why each of its hypotheses is needed
  • Find infinite limits and limits at infinity, and the vertical, horizontal and oblique asymptotes of a graph
  • Compare the growth of logarithms, powers, exponentials and factorials, and use big-O notation
1

Continuity at a point

A cup of tea cooling from 80 °C to 60 °C passes through every temperature in between, because temperature changes gradually. A car park’s charge does not. Suppose (hypothetically) that a car park charges £3 for each hour or part of an hour: 59 minutes cost £3, 61 minutes cost £6, and no length of stay costs £4.50. The charge jumps.

Module 2 met three ways for a limit to fail to exist: a jump, a blow-up and an oscillation. This module asks the opposite question: when is the limit at each point equal to the value there? Such a function is continuous, and on an interval its graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil. Continuity guarantees that equations have solutions (Section 3.3), which can be found to any accuracy (Section 3.4), and that largest and smallest values exist (Section 3.5). Sections 3.6 to 3.8 then follow functions to infinity.

Definition 3.1Continuity at a point

Let fff be defined on an open interval that contains a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, except perhaps at aaa itself. Then fff is continuous at aaa if

lim⁡x→af(x)=f(a).\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a).x→alim​f(x)=f(a).

This asks for three things:

  1. f(a)f(a)f(a) is defined;
  2. lim⁡x→af(x)\lim_{x\to a} f(x)limx→a​f(x) exists;
  3. the limit equals the value.

If fff is not continuous at a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, then fff is discontinuous at a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, and aaa is a discontinuity of f.f\mathclose{\text{.}}f.

In words: inputs close to aaa give outputs close to f(a),f(a)\mathclose{\text{,}}f(a), and the graph does not break at (a,f(a)).(a, f(a))\mathclose{\text{.}}(a,f(a)). In the ε–δ language of Module 2: for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is a δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that

∣f(x)−f(a)∣<εwhenever∣x−a∣<δ.\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon \quad\text{whenever}\quad \abs{x - a} < \delta.∣f(x)−f(a)∣<εwhenever∣x−a∣<δ.

(The limit only looks at x≠a,x \ne a\mathclose{\text{,}}x=a, but x=ax = ax=a does no harm here, since ∣f(a)−f(a)∣=0.)\abs{f(a) - f(a)} = 0\mathclose{\text{.)}}∣f(a)−f(a)∣=0.)

Example 3.1Testing the three conditions✓ Checked

Decide whether each function is continuous at 2. If it is not, say which condition fails.

  • (a) f(x)=x2−4x−2f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}f(x)=x−2x2−4​
  • (b) g(x)=x2−4x−2g(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}g(x)=x−2x2−4​ for x≠2,x \ne 2\mathclose{\text{,}}x=2, and g(2)=1g(2) = 1g(2)=1
  • (c) the function hhh above
  • (d) the function kkk above

(a) Condition 1 fails: f(2)=0/0f(2) = 0/0f(2)=0/0 is not defined. So fff is discontinuous at 2, although its limit there exists: for x≠2,x \ne 2\mathclose{\text{,}}x=2, f(x)=(x−2)(x+2)x−2=x+2,f(x) = \dfrac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{x - 2} = x + 2\mathclose{\text{,}}f(x)=x−2(x−2)(x+2)​=x+2, so lim⁡x→2f(x)=4.\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) = 4\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→2​f(x)=4.

(b) Now g(2)=1g(2) = 1g(2)=1 is defined, and the limit exists and is 4, as in (a): conditions 1 and 2 hold. Condition 3 fails, since 4≠1.4 \ne 1\mathclose{\text{.}}4=1. So ggg is discontinuous at 2.

(c) h(2)=6−2=4.h(2) = 6 - 2 = 4\mathclose{\text{.}}h(2)=6−2=4. The formula changes at 2, so use one-sided limits (Module 2): from the left lim⁡x→2−x2=4,\lim_{x\to 2^-} x^2 = 4\mathclose{\text{,}}limx→2−​x2=4, and from the right lim⁡x→2+(6−x)=4.\lim_{x\to2^+} (6 - x) = 4\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→2+​(6−x)=4. They agree, so lim⁡x→2h(x)=4=h(2):\lim_{x\to2} h(x) = 4 = h(2)\mathclose{\text{:}}limx→2​h(x)=4=h(2): all three conditions hold, and hhh is continuous at 2, although it is given by two formulas.

(d) From the left the limit is 4 again; from the right it is lim⁡x→2+(5−x)=3.\lim_{x\to2^+}(5 - x) = 3\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→2+​(5−x)=3. The one-sided limits differ, so condition 2 fails: kkk is discontinuous at 2, although k(2)=3k(2) = 3k(2)=3 is defined.

Watch out

Two opposite mistakes. Being defined at aaa and having a limit at aaa is not enough: the limit must equal the value, as (b) shows. And a formula in several pieces is no sign of a discontinuity: hhh in (c) is continuous at 2 because its pieces meet there. Check the three conditions; do not judge by the look of the formula.

One-sided continuity

Some functions jump, yet their value at the jump fits one of the two sides, like the floor function. The floor of x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, written ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor⌊x⌋ and read “floor xxx”, is the largest integer less than or equal to x:x\mathclose{\text{:}}x: ⌊2.7⌋=2,\lfloor 2.7\rfloor = 2\mathclose{\text{,}}⌊2.7⌋=2, ⌊3⌋=3\lfloor 3\rfloor = 3⌊3⌋=3 and ⌊−2.7⌋=−3.\lfloor -2.7\rfloor = -3\mathclose{\text{.}}⌊−2.7⌋=−3. In Python it is math.floor, and integer division 7 // 2 gives ⌊7/2⌋=3.\lfloor 7/2\rfloor = 3\mathclose{\text{.}}⌊7/2⌋=3. Its graph is a staircase. At x=3:x = 3\mathclose{\text{:}}x=3: for xxx slightly less than 3, ⌊x⌋=2,\lfloor x\rfloor = 2\mathclose{\text{,}}⌊x⌋=2, and for 3≤x<4,3 \le x < 4\mathclose{\text{,}}3≤x<4, ⌊x⌋=3.\lfloor x\rfloor = 3\mathclose{\text{.}}⌊x⌋=3. So

lim⁡x→3−⌊x⌋=2,lim⁡x→3+⌊x⌋=3=⌊3⌋.\lim_{x\to3^-}\lfloor x\rfloor = 2, \qquad \lim_{x\to3^+}\lfloor x\rfloor = 3 = \lfloor 3\rfloor.x→3−lim​⌊x⌋=2,x→3+lim​⌊x⌋=3=⌊3⌋.

The limit at 3 does not exist, so the floor function is discontinuous at 3; but its value agrees with the limit from the right.

Definition 3.2One-sided continuity and continuity on an interval

A function fff is continuous from the right at aaa if lim⁡x→a+f(x)=f(a),\lim_{x\to a^+} f(x) = f(a)\mathclose{\text{,}}limx→a+​f(x)=f(a), and continuous from the left at aaa if lim⁡x→a−f(x)=f(a).\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) = f(a)\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→a−​f(x)=f(a).

fff is continuous on an interval III if it is continuous at every number of I,I\mathclose{\text{,}}I, except that at an endpoint that belongs to III it need only be continuous from the side of I:I\mathclose{\text{:}}I: from the right at a left endpoint, from the left at a right endpoint.

So ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor⌊x⌋ is continuous from the right at every integer, and continuous on each interval [n,n+1),[n, n + 1)\mathclose{\text{,}}[n,n+1), but not on [n,n+1]:[n, n + 1]\mathclose{\text{:}}[n,n+1]: at n+1n + 1n+1 it is not continuous from the left. The square root is defined only for x≥0,x \ge 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x≥0, so at 0 only one side counts: lim⁡x→0+x=0=0,\lim_{x\to0^+}\sqrt x = 0 = \sqrt0\mathclose{\text{,}}limx→0+​x​=0=0​, and x\sqrt xx​ is continuous on [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞) (Section 3.2). Since a limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal (Module 2), fff is continuous at aaa exactly when it is continuous from both sides there.

Staircases are everywhere in computing: a digital thermometer that shows whole degrees, rounding down, displays ⌊T⌋\lfloor T\rfloor⌊T⌋ for a true temperature T,T\mathclose{\text{,}}T, and its reading jumps at every whole degree.

Watch out

Read one-sided continuity off the graph. Each step of y=⌊x⌋y = \lfloor x\rfloory=⌊x⌋ has its filled dot at its left end, (n,n),(n, n)\mathclose{\text{,}}(n,n), and runs to the right from there: so ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor⌊x⌋ is continuous from the right. Calling it “continuous from the left” because the dot is on the left is the usual slip.

Kinds of discontinuity

Discontinuities come in a few kinds (Figure 3.1), named after what the graph does near the point.

Definition 3.3Kinds of discontinuity

Let aaa be a discontinuity of f.f\mathclose{\text{.}}f. The discontinuity is

  • removable if lim⁡x→af(x)\lim_{x\to a} f(x)limx→a​f(x) exists;
  • a jump if both one-sided limits exist but are different;
  • infinite if, as xxx approaches aaa from at least one side, the values f(x)f(x)f(x) become, and stay, larger than any number you name, or smaller than any number you name (Section 3.6 writes this lim⁡x→a+f(x)=∞,\lim_{x\to a^+} f(x) = \infty\mathclose{\text{,}}limx→a+​f(x)=∞, lim⁡x→a−f(x)=−∞,\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) = -\infty\mathclose{\text{,}}limx→a−​f(x)=−∞, and so on);
  • oscillating in every other case: then at least one one-sided limit fails to exist without becoming infinite, as when fff keeps swinging between values.

A removable discontinuity is removed by defining, or redefining, fff at the single point a:a\mathclose{\text{:}}a: set f(a)=lim⁡x→af(x).f(a) = \lim_{x\to a} f(x)\mathclose{\text{.}}f(a)=limx→a​f(x). That repairs ggg of Example 3.1: give it the value 4 at 2. No single value repairs the other three kinds, because at them lim⁡x→af(x)\lim_{x\to a} f(x)limx→a​f(x) does not exist.

Example 3.2Classifying discontinuities✓ Checked

Find and classify the discontinuities of

  • (a) r(x)=x2−4x2−x−2,r(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x^2 - x - 2}\mathclose{\text{,}}r(x)=x2−x−2x2−4​, the rational function of Example 1.5;
  • (b) s(x)=∣x∣x;s(x) = \dfrac{\abs{x}}{x}\mathclose{\text{;}}s(x)=x∣x∣​;
  • (c) q(x)=sin⁡xx.q(x) = \dfrac{\sin x}{x}\mathclose{\text{.}}q(x)=xsinx​.

(a) Module 1 factored top and bottom: r(x)=(x−2)(x+2)(x−2)(x+1).r(x) = \dfrac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{(x - 2)(x + 1)}\mathclose{\text{.}}r(x)=(x−2)(x+1)(x−2)(x+2)​. So rrr is not defined at 2 and at −1,-1\mathclose{\text{,}}−1, and r(x)=x+2x+1r(x) = \dfrac{x + 2}{x + 1}r(x)=x+1x+2​ for every other x;x\mathclose{\text{;}}x; Section 3.2 shows that rrr is continuous everywhere except at these two numbers. At 2, by direct substitution in the cancelled form,

lim⁡x→2r(x)=lim⁡x→2x+2x+1=43,\lim_{x\to2} r(x) = \lim_{x\to2}\frac{x + 2}{x + 1} = \frac43,x→2lim​r(x)=x→2lim​x+1x+2​=34​,

At −1,-1\mathclose{\text{,}}−1, the numerator x+2x + 2x+2 approaches 1 and the denominator x+1x + 1x+1 approaches 0, so the values of rrr grow without bound: an infinite discontinuity (Section 3.6 finds the one-sided limits).

(b) sss is not defined at 0. It is −1-1−1 for x<0x < 0x<0 and 111 for x>0,x > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x>0, so, as Module 2 found, lim⁡x→0−s(x)=−1\lim_{x\to0^-} s(x) = -1limx→0−​s(x)=−1 and lim⁡x→0+s(x)=1:\lim_{x\to0^+} s(x) = 1\mathclose{\text{:}}limx→0+​s(x)=1: 0 is a jump discontinuity.

(c) qqq is not defined at 0, and Module 2 proved that lim⁡x→0sin⁡xx=1.\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sin x}{x} = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→0​xsinx​=1. So 0 is a removable discontinuity: sin⁡xx,\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\mathclose{\text{,}}xsinx​, given the value 1 at 0, is continuous at 0. This repaired function is the sinc function of signal processing (some books put πx\pi xπx in place of x).x\mathclose{\text{).}}x).

Watch out

A zero in the denominator does not always mean an infinite discontinuity: the denominator of rrr is 0 at 2, but so is the numerator, the factor x−2x - 2x−2 cancels, and the discontinuity is removable. Factor and cancel first, then decide. And the kind depends on the limits near a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, not on f(a):f(a)\mathclose{\text{:}}f(a): sss and qqq are both undefined at 0, but differ in kind.

Which functions are continuous

Checking three conditions at every point would never end. A few theorems settle continuity at once for every function built from the catalogue of Module 1.

Sums, products and quotients

Theorem 3.1Continuity laws

If fff and ggg are continuous at aaa and ccc is a constant, then the functions

f+g,f−g,cf,fgf + g, \qquad f - g, \qquad cf, \qquad fgf+g,f−g,cf,fg

are continuous at a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, and so is f/gf/gf/g if g(a)≠0.g(a) \ne 0\mathclose{\text{.}}g(a)=0. The same holds for continuity from one side, and so for continuity on an interval.

Proof

Each statement is a limit law of Module 2 in disguise. For the product: since lim⁡x→af(x)=f(a)\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)limx→a​f(x)=f(a) and lim⁡x→ag(x)=g(a),\lim_{x\to a} g(x) = g(a)\mathclose{\text{,}}limx→a​g(x)=g(a), the product law gives

lim⁡x→af(x) g(x)=lim⁡x→af(x)⋅lim⁡x→ag(x)=f(a) g(a),\begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to a} f(x)\,g(x) &= \lim_{x\to a} f(x) \cdot \lim_{x\to a} g(x) \\ &= f(a)\,g(a), \end{aligned}x→alim​f(x)g(x)​=x→alim​f(x)⋅x→alim​g(x)=f(a)g(a),​

which says that fgfgfg is continuous at a.a\mathclose{\text{.}}a. Sums, differences and constant multiples work the same way. The quotient law needs the limit of the denominator to be non-zero, and it is: lim⁡x→ag(x)=g(a)≠0.\lim_{x\to a} g(x) = g(a) \ne 0\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→a​g(x)=g(a)=0. (So g(x)≠0g(x) \ne 0g(x)=0 for xxx close to a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, and f/gf/gf/g is defined on an open interval around a.)a\mathclose{\text{.)}}a.) One-sided limits obey the same laws, which gives the one-sided statements.

∎
Theorem 3.2Polynomials and rational functions

Every polynomial is continuous on R.\R\mathclose{\text{.}}R. Every rational function is continuous at every number of its domain.

Proof

This is the direct substitution theorem of Module 2 in new words. For a polynomial ppp and every number a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, lim⁡x→ap(x)=p(a).\lim_{x\to a} p(x) = p(a)\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→a​p(x)=p(a). For a rational function p/qp/qp/q and a number aaa of its domain, q(a)≠0,q(a) \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}q(a)=0, and lim⁡x→ap(x)/q(x)=p(a)/q(a).\lim_{x\to a} p(x)/q(x) = p(a)/q(a)\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→a​p(x)/q(x)=p(a)/q(a). Each statement says that the limit is the value: continuity at a.a\mathclose{\text{.}}a.

∎

This completes Example 3.2: rrr is continuous at every number except 2 and −1.-1\mathclose{\text{.}}−1.

The catalogue is continuous

Theorem 3.3Continuity of the standard functions

Each of these functions is continuous at every number of its domain (at 0, the endpoint of the domain of an even root, from the right):

  • roots xn,\sqrt[n]{x}\mathclose{\text{,}}nx​, for whole numbers n≥2;n \ge 2\mathclose{\text{;}}n≥2;
  • the trigonometric functions sin⁡x,\sin x\mathclose{\text{,}}sinx, cos⁡x,\cos x\mathclose{\text{,}}cosx, tan⁡x,\tan x\mathclose{\text{,}}tanx, cot⁡x,\cot x\mathclose{\text{,}}cotx, sec⁡x\sec xsecx and csc⁡x;\csc x\mathclose{\text{;}}cscx;
  • exponential functions ax,a^x\mathclose{\text{,}}ax, for a>0;a > 0\mathclose{\text{;}}a>0;
  • logarithms log⁡ax,\log_a x\mathclose{\text{,}}loga​x, for a>0a > 0a>0 with a≠1;a \ne 1\mathclose{\text{;}}a=1; in particular ln⁡x.\ln x\mathclose{\text{.}}lnx.

Here is why, family by family: proofs for sine, cosine and roots, and the idea of the proof for exponentials and logarithms. On a first reading you may take the theorem on trust.

Sine and cosine. Module 2 proved that sin⁡h→0=sin⁡0\sin h \to 0 = \sin 0sinh→0=sin0 and cos⁡h→1=cos⁡0\cos h \to 1 = \cos 0cosh→1=cos0 as h→0:h \to 0\mathclose{\text{:}}h→0: sine and cosine are continuous at 0. For any other number a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, write x=a+h,x = a + h\mathclose{\text{,}}x=a+h, so that h→0h \to 0h→0 as x→a.x \to a\mathclose{\text{.}}x→a. The addition formula of Section 1.4 and those two limits give

sin⁡(a+h)=sin⁡acos⁡h+cos⁡asin⁡h→sin⁡a⋅1+cos⁡a⋅0=sin⁡a.\begin{aligned} \sin(a + h) &= \sin a\cos h + \cos a\sin h \\ &\to \sin a \cdot 1 + \cos a \cdot 0 = \sin a. \end{aligned}sin(a+h)​=sinacosh+cosasinh→sina⋅1+cosa⋅0=sina.​

In the same way cos⁡(a+h)=cos⁡acos⁡h−sin⁡asin⁡h→cos⁡a.\cos(a + h) = \cos a\cos h - \sin a\sin h \to \cos a\mathclose{\text{.}}cos(a+h)=cosacosh−sinasinh→cosa. So sine and cosine are continuous on R,\R\mathclose{\text{,}}R, and the other four, quotients built from these two, are continuous wherever their denominators are not 0 (Theorem 3.1): on their domains.

Roots. By the root law of Module 2, lim⁡x→axn=an\lim_{x\to a}\sqrt[n]{x} = \sqrt[n]{a}limx→a​nx​=na​ for every a>0,a > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}a>0, and for every aaa when nnn is odd. At 0 an even root is continuous from the right: xn<ε\sqrt[n]{x} < \varepsilonnx​<ε whenever 0≤x<εn,0 \le x < \varepsilon^n\mathclose{\text{,}}0≤x<εn, which is the ε–δ condition with δ=εn.\delta = \varepsilon^n\mathclose{\text{.}}δ=εn.

Exponentials and logarithms. For an irrational xxx such as 2,\sqrt2\mathclose{\text{,}}2​, Module 1 defined axa^xax as the number that a1.4,a1.41,a1.414,…a^{1.4}, a^{1.41}, a^{1.414}, \dotsa1.4,a1.41,a1.414,… approach. Making that precise is what shows axa^xax to be continuous; it belongs to a course in analysis, and this series takes it as known. The logarithm log⁡a\log_aloga​ is the inverse of ax,a^x\mathclose{\text{,}}ax, so its graph is the mirror image of the graph of axa^xax in the line y=xy = xy=x (Theorem 1.2), and the mirror image of an unbroken curve is unbroken. That is the idea behind a fact proved in analysis courses: the inverse of a continuous function that is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on an interval (Exercise 1.10) is continuous.

Key idea

Every function built from the catalogue of Module 1 with +,+\mathclose{\text{,}}+, −,-\mathclose{\text{,}}−, ×,\times\mathclose{\text{,}}×, ÷\div÷ and composition (below) is continuous on every interval that lies in its domain. A discontinuity can only occur where a formula breaks down (a zero denominator, the logarithm of 0) or where a piecewise definition changes formula.

Watch out

“Continuous on its domain” is not “continuous everywhere”. 1/x1/x1/x and tan⁡x\tan xtanx are continuous at every number of their domains, and books call them continuous functions; yet they have infinite discontinuities at 0 and at π/2,\pi/2\mathclose{\text{,}}π/2, outside their domains, where their graphs break. Asked where a function is continuous, give the intervals: 1/x1/x1/x is continuous on (−∞,0)(-\infty, 0)(−∞,0) and on (0,∞),(0, \infty)\mathclose{\text{,}}(0,∞), but not on [−1,1].[-1, 1]\mathclose{\text{.}}[−1,1].

Composition

Most formulas nest one function inside another: 9−x2,\sqrt{9 - x^2}\mathclose{\text{,}}9−x2​, ln⁡(1+cos⁡x),\ln(1 + \cos x)\mathclose{\text{,}}ln(1+cosx), e(sin⁡x)/x.e^{(\sin x)/x}\mathclose{\text{.}}e(sinx)/x. Limits can be moved inside such a nest, as long as the outer function is continuous.

Theorem 3.4Limits of compositions

3

The Intermediate Value Theorem

Walk up a mountain path from a hut at 1200 m to a summit at 2100 m. However the path twists and dips, at some moment you are at exactly 1500 m: your height changes continuously, so it cannot skip from below 1500 m to above it. In the same way, a horizontal line at any height NNN between f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b) must meet the graph of a continuous function somewhere between aaa and bbb (Figure 3.2).

Theorem 3.6The Intermediate Value Theorem

Suppose that fff is continuous on the closed interval [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b], and let NNN be any number strictly between f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b).f(b)\mathclose{\text{.}}f(b). Then there is at least one number ccc in (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) with f(c)=N.f(c) = N\mathclose{\text{.}}f(c)=N.

The form you will use most is about roots. If fff is continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b] and f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b) have opposite signs, then 0 lies strictly between them, so the equation f(x)=0f(x) = 0f(x)=0 has a solution in (a,b).(a, b)\mathclose{\text{.}}(a,b).

The hypothesis is continuity on the whole closed interval, endpoints included, and every part of it is needed:

  • Without continuity. Let f(x)=−1f(x) = -1f(x)=−1 for x<0x < 0x<0 and f(x)=1f(x) = 1f(x)=1 for x≥0.x \ge 0\mathclose{\text{.}}x≥0. On [−1,1],[-1, 1]\mathclose{\text{,}}[−1,1], f(−1)=−1<0<1=f(1),f(-1) = -1 < 0 < 1 = f(1)\mathclose{\text{,}}f(−1)=−1<0<1=f(1), but fff is never 0: the jump at 0 skips every value strictly between −1-1−1 and 1.
  • Without continuity at an endpoint. Let g(0)=−1g(0) = -1g(0)=−1 and g(x)=xg(x) = xg(x)=x for 0<x≤1.0 < x \le 1\mathclose{\text{.}}0<x≤1. Then ggg is continuous on (0,1],(0, 1]\mathclose{\text{,}}(0,1], and g(0)=−1<0<1=g(1),g(0) = -1 < 0 < 1 = g(1)\mathclose{\text{,}}g(0)=−1<0<1=g(1), but g(x)=xg(x) = xg(x)=x is positive for every xxx in (0,1]:(0, 1]\mathclose{\text{:}}(0,1]: ggg has no root. The culprit is the endpoint 0, where ggg is not continuous from the right, since lim⁡x→0+g(x)=0≠g(0).\lim_{x\to0^+} g(x) = 0 \ne g(0)\mathclose{\text{.}}limx→0+​g(x)=0=g(0).

Notice also what the theorem does not say. It promises at least one c,c\mathclose{\text{,}}c, not exactly one: in Figure 3.2 there are three. And it does not say where ccc is: it is an existence theorem. Section 3.4 turns it into a method for finding c.c\mathclose{\text{.}}c.

Going deeperWhy the Intermediate Value Theorem is true

A first reading may skip this proof. It takes one property of the real numbers as an axiom, and proves the rest.

Suppose that fff is continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b] and f(a)<N<f(b).f(a) < N < f(b)\mathclose{\text{.}}f(a)<N<f(b). (If f(a)>N>f(b),f(a) > N > f(b)\mathclose{\text{,}}f(a)>N>f(b), apply the argument to −f-f−f and −N.)-N\mathclose{\text{.)}}−N.) Halve [a,b].[a, b]\mathclose{\text{.}}[a,b]. If fff takes the value NNN at the midpoint, that midpoint is the ccc wanted; otherwise keep the half at whose left end fff is below NNN and at whose right end it is above. Repeat. Either some midpoint gives the value N,N\mathclose{\text{,}}N, or you get intervals [an,bn],[a_n, b_n]\mathclose{\text{,}}[an​,bn​], each half the one before, with f(an)<N<f(bn)f(a_n) < N < f(b_n)f(an​)<N<f(bn​) for every n:n\mathclose{\text{:}}n: the bisection method of the next section, with NNN in place of 0.

The left ends a0≤a1≤a2≤⋯a_0 \le a_1 \le a_2 \le \cdotsa0​≤a1​≤a2​≤⋯ never decrease, the right ends b0≥b1≥b2≥⋯b_0 \ge b_1 \ge b_2 \ge \cdotsb0​≥b1​≥b2​≥⋯ never increase, and the width bn−an=(b−a)/2nb_n - a_n = (b - a)/2^nbn​−an​=(b−a)/2n shrinks to 0. Here the proof needs the completeness of the real numbers: the number line has no gaps, so some number ccc lies in every one of the intervals, an≤c≤bna_n \le c \le b_nan​≤c≤bn​ for every n.n\mathclose{\text{.}}n. This is the axiom. (Module 14 states it as the Monotone Convergence Theorem: a sequence that never decreases and stays below a fixed bound has a limit. Here ccc is the limit of the an.)a_n\mathclose{\text{.)}}an​.)

It remains to show that f(c)=N.f(c) = N\mathclose{\text{.}}f(c)=N. Suppose not, and challenge the continuity of fff at ccc with ε=∣f(c)−N∣.\varepsilon = \abs{f(c) - N}\mathclose{\text{.}}ε=∣f(c)−N∣. There is a δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that ∣f(x)−f(c)∣<ε\abs{f(x) - f(c)} < \varepsilon∣f(x)−f(c)∣<ε for every xxx in [a,b][a, b][a,b] with ∣x−c∣<δ:\abs{x - c} < \delta\mathclose{\text{:}}∣x−c∣<δ: all those f(x)f(x)f(x) are closer to f(c)f(c)f(c) than NNN is, so they lie on the same side of NNN as f(c).f(c)\mathclose{\text{.}}f(c). Take nnn so large that bn−an<δ.b_n - a_n < \delta\mathclose{\text{.}}bn​−an​<δ. Since ccc lies in [an,bn],[a_n, b_n]\mathclose{\text{,}}[an​,bn​], both ends are within δ\deltaδ of c,c\mathclose{\text{,}}c, so f(an)f(a_n)f(an​) and f(bn)f(b_n)f(bn​) lie on the same side of N.N\mathclose{\text{.}}N. But f(an)<N<f(bn).f(a_n) < N < f(b_n)\mathclose{\text{.}}f(an​)<N<f(bn​). So f(c)=N.f(c) = N\mathclose{\text{.}}f(c)=N. Finally, ccc is neither aaa nor b,b\mathclose{\text{,}}b, because f(a)≠N≠f(b).f(a) \ne N \ne f(b)\mathclose{\text{.}}f(a)=N=f(b).

Completeness is essential. Within the rational numbers alone the theorem is false: x2−2x^2 - 2x2−2 is negative at 1 and positive at 2, but no rational number ccc has c2=2,c^2 = 2\mathclose{\text{,}}c2=2, because 2\sqrt22​ is irrational; the intervals [an,bn][a_n, b_n][an​,bn​] close in on the gap where 2\sqrt22​ would be. Courses in real analysis either build the real numbers and prove completeness, or take it as an axiom, as here.

4

The bisection method

The Intermediate Value Theorem says that x3−2x−5x^3 - 2x - 5x3−2x−5 has a root in (2,3),(2, 3)\mathclose{\text{,}}(2,3), but not where. The bisection method finds it by applying the theorem again and again: halve the interval, and keep the half where the sign changes.

Definition 3.4The bisection method

Let fff be continuous on [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b], with f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b) of opposite signs. Start with the bracket [a0,b0]=[a,b].[a_0, b_0] = [a, b]\mathclose{\text{.}}[a0​,b0​]=[a,b]. For n=0,1,2,…:n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\mathclose{\text{:}}n=0,1,2,…:

  1. Compute the midpoint mn=an+bn2m_n = \dfrac{a_n + b_n}{2}mn​=2an​+bn​​ and the value f(mn).f(m_n)\mathclose{\text{.}}f(mn​).
  2. If f(mn)=0,f(m_n) = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}f(mn​)=0, stop: mnm_nmn​ is a root.
  3. If f(mn)f(m_n)f(mn​) has the same sign as f(an),f(a_n)\mathclose{\text{,}}f(an​), the new bracket is [an+1,bn+1]=[mn,bn];[a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}] = [m_n, b_n]\mathclose{\text{;}}[an+1​,bn+1​]=[mn​,bn​]; otherwise it is [an+1,bn+1]=[an,mn].[a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}] = [a_n, m_n]\mathclose{\text{.}}[an+1​,bn+1​]=[an​,mn​].

Stop when the bracket is as narrow as you need.

Read ana_nan​ as “a sub n”. Step 3 always keeps a half at whose ends fff has opposite signs, so, by the Intermediate Value Theorem, every bracket contains a root (Figure 3.3).

Example 3.72\sqrt22​ by bisection✓ Checked

Theorem 3.7The error of the bisection method

Let fff be continuous on [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b], with f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b) of opposite signs. If the bisection method has not stopped at an exact root, then after nnn steps the bracket [an,bn][a_n, b_n][an​,bn​] contains a root rrr of f,f\mathclose{\text{,}}f, and

bn−an=b−a2n,∣mn−r∣≤b−a2n+1.b_n - a_n = \frac{b - a}{2^n}, \quad \abs{m_n - r} \le \frac{b - a}{2^{n+1}}.bn​−an​=2nb−a​,∣mn​−r∣≤2n+1b−a​.
Proof

Each step gains one binary digit. Since 210=1024≈103,2^{10} = 1024 \approx 10^3\mathclose{\text{,}}210=1024≈103, ten steps gain about three decimal digits, so each decimal digit costs about 3.33.33.3 steps. Bisection is binary search on the number line, and the count is the one of Section 1.4: binary search in a sorted list of a million items takes about 20 steps for the same reason.

Strengths and weaknesses. Bisection always works when its hypotheses hold, with a guaranteed error. But it is slow, one binary digit per step whatever the function; Newton’s method (Module 7) usually doubles the number of correct digits at every step, though it can fail. Bisection needs a sign change, so it cannot find a root where the graph touches the axis without crossing it, as (x−1)2(x - 1)^2(x−1)2 does at 1; and when a bracket contains several roots, it finds only one.

Compute itThe bisection method in Python

The method takes a few lines of Python. This function runs n steps and returns the final bracket, or the pair (m, m) if it meets an exact root m:

Python
def bisection(f, a, b, n):
    """n steps of the bisection method on [a, b]; returns the last bracket."""
    if f(a) * f(b) >= 0:
        raise ValueError("f(a) and f(b) must have opposite signs")
    for _ in range(n):
        m = (a + b) / 2
        if f(m) == 0:
            return m, m                    # an exact root
        if (f(m) > 0) == (f(a) > 0):       # same sign as f(a): keep [m, b]
            a = m
        else:                              # otherwise keep [a, m]
            b = m
    return a, b

print(bisection(lambda x: x**2 - 2, 1, 2, 6))
Output
(1.40625, 1.421875)

That is the bracket [a6,b6][a_6, b_6][a6​,b6​] of Example 3.7. By Example 3.8, 19 steps give 2\sqrt22​ to within 10−6;10^{-6}\mathclose{\text{;}}10−6; compare the midpoint’s real error with the guarantee 2−20:2^{-20}\mathclose{\text{:}}2−20:

Python
import math
a, b = bisection(lambda x: x**2 - 2, 1, 2, 19)
m = (a + b) / 2
print(m, abs(m - math.sqrt(2)), 2**-20)
Output
1.4142141342163086 5.718432134482754e-07 9.5367431640625e-07

The real error is smaller than the guarantee, as it often is. The same function solves the equations of Examples 3.5 and 3.6, x3−2x−5=0x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0x3−2x−5=0 and cos⁡x=x.\cos x = x\mathclose{\text{.}}cosx=x. a, b = bisection(lambda x: x**3 - 2*x - 5, 2, 3, 30)
print((a + b) / 2)
a, b = bisection(lambda x: math.cos(x) - x, 0, 1, 30)
print((a + b) / 2)

0.7390851336531341

The Extreme Value Theorem

Over a whole day, from midnight to midnight, the outside temperature has a highest value and a lowest value, each reached at some moment of the day. That is not a fact about the weather: it holds for every continuous function on a closed interval.

Definition 3.5Maximum and minimum values

Let fff be defined on an interval I.I\mathclose{\text{.}}I. The number f(c),f(c)\mathclose{\text{,}}f(c), for a ccc in I,I\mathclose{\text{,}}I, is the maximum value of fff on III if f(x)≤f(c)f(x) \le f(c)f(x)≤f(c) for every xxx in I.I\mathclose{\text{.}}I. The number f(d),f(d)\mathclose{\text{,}}f(d), for a ddd in I,I\mathclose{\text{,}}I, is the minimum value of fff on III if f(x)≥f(d)f(x) \ge f(d)f(x)≥f(d) for every xxx in I.I\mathclose{\text{.}}I. Together they are the extreme values of fff on I.I\mathclose{\text{.}}I.

A maximum value must be a value: a number f(c)f(c)f(c) that fff actually takes, not merely a number that the values approach. Module 8 calls these the absolute maximum and minimum, and finds them with derivatives.

Theorem 3.8The Extreme Value Theorem

If fff is continuous on a closed interval [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b], then fff has a maximum value and a minimum value on [a,b]:[a, b]\mathclose{\text{:}}[a,b]: there are numbers ccc and ddd in [a,b][a, b][a,b] such that, for every xxx in [a,b],[a, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[a,b],

f(d)≤f(x)≤f(c).f(d) \le f(x) \le f(c).f(d)≤f(x)≤f(c).

Its proof also rests on the completeness of the real numbers, but takes more work than the proof of the Intermediate Value Theorem; it belongs to a course in real analysis, and this series uses the theorem without proof. What you can see now is why each hypothesis is needed (Figure 3.4):

  • A closed interval. f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x is continuous on the open interval (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) but has no maximum value there: for any xxx in (0,1),(0, 1)\mathclose{\text{,}}(0,1), the number x+12\tfrac{x + 1}{2}2x+1​ is in (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) too, and larger. The values approach 1, but the end where they would reach it is missing. Likewise there is no minimum value.
  • Continuity. On [0,1],[0, 1]\mathclose{\text{,}}[0,1], let f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x for 0≤x<10 \le x < 10≤x<1 and f(1)=0.f(1) = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}f(1)=0. Again the values approach 1 without reaching it: at 1, where fff is not continuous from the left, the value drops to 0. This fff has the minimum value 0, but no maximum value.
  • A bounded interval. [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞) contains its endpoint but has no right end, so it is not a closed interval [a,b].[a, b]\mathclose{\text{.}}[a,b]. On it, f(x)=xx+1=1−1x+1f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x + 1} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{x + 1}f(x)=x+1x​=1−x+11​ is continuous, and it increases as xxx increases, creeping up towards 1 (Section 3.7) without reaching it. Every value is beaten by a later one: no maximum value.

The theorem says that extreme values exist, not where: at an end of the interval, like the maximum in Figure 3.4, or inside it, like the minimum. In optimisation it guarantees that a best choice exists: a cost that depends continuously on a setting has a cheapest setting in every closed interval of settings. Module 8 shows how to find it.

Example 3.9Does the theorem apply?✓ Checked

Decide whether the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees a maximum and a minimum value, and find them where you can.

  • (a) f(x)=x2−4x+1f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 1f(x)=x2−4x+1 on [0,3][0, 3][0,3]
  • (b) g(x)=1x−1g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 1}g(x)=x−11​ on [2,4][2, 4][2,4]
  • (c) the same ggg on [0,2][0, 2][0,2]

(a) fff is a polynomial, continuous on the closed interval [0,3],[0, 3]\mathclose{\text{,}}[0,3], so the theorem guarantees both. To find them, complete the square: f(x)=(x−2)2−3.f(x) = (x - 2)^2 - 3\mathclose{\text{.}}f(x)=(x−2)2−3. Since (x−2)2≥0,(x - 2)^2 \ge 0\mathclose{\text{,}}(x−2)2≥0, with equality only at x=2,x = 2\mathclose{\text{,}}x=2, the minimum value is f(2)=−3.f(2) = -3\mathclose{\text{.}}f(2)=−3. On [0,3],[0, 3]\mathclose{\text{,}}[0,3], (x−2)2(x - 2)^2(x−2)2 is largest where xxx is farthest from 2, at x=0,x = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x=0, so the maximum value is f(0)=1.f(0) = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}f(0)=1. As xxx increases, x−1x - 1x−1 increases and 1x−1\dfrac{1}{x - 1}x−11​ decreases, so the maximum value is g(2)=1g(2) = 1g(2)=1 and the minimum value is g(4)=13.g(4) = \tfrac13\mathclose{\text{.}}g(4)=31​.

(c) ggg is not defined at 1, which lies in [0,2],[0, 2]\mathclose{\text{,}}[0,2], so ggg is not continuous on [0,2],[0, 2]\mathclose{\text{,}}[0,2], and the theorem does not apply. Watch out

Two slips. “fff is continuous on (0,1),(0, 1)\mathclose{\text{,}}(0,1), so it has a maximum” is wrong, as f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x shows: the theorem needs a closed interval [a,b].[a, b]\mathclose{\text{.}}[a,b]. And when the hypotheses fail, the theorem says nothing either way: on the open interval (−1,2),(-1, 2)\mathclose{\text{,}}(−1,2), x2x^2x2 has the minimum value 0, though no maximum value.

To find the limit of a rational function at infinity, divide the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of xxx in the denominator; then every term with xxx left in its denominator tends to 0. Only the leading terms matter:

Watch out

A graph can cross its horizontal asymptote, even infinitely often: sin⁡xx\dfrac{\sin x}{x}xsinx​ is 0 at every non-zero multiple of π.\pi\mathclose{\text{.}}π. An asymptote describes the graph far out; it is not a line that the graph never touches.

Oblique asymptotes

When the degree of the numerator is one more than that of the denominator, a rational function grows without bound, but in a definite direction: its graph approaches a slanted line.

Definition 3.8Oblique asymptote

The line y=mx+c,y = mx + c\mathclose{\text{,}}y=mx+c, with m≠0,m \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}m=0, is an oblique asymptote (or slant asymptote) of the graph of fff if

lim⁡x→∞[f(x)−(mx+c)]=0orlim⁡x→−∞[f(x)−(mx+c)]=0.\begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to\infty}\big[f(x) - (mx + c)\big] &= 0 \quad\text{or} \\ \lim_{x\to-\infty}\big[f(x) - (mx + c)\big] &= 0. \end{aligned}x→∞lim​[f(x)−(mx+c)]x→−∞lim​[f(x)−(mx+c)]​=0or=0.​

The bracket is the vertical distance between the graph and the line, and it shrinks to 0. For a rational function p/qp/qp/q whose numerator has degree one more than its denominator, divide: p(x)=q(x)(mx+c)+s(x),p(x) = q(x)(mx + c) + s(x)\mathclose{\text{,}}p(x)=q(x)(mx+c)+s(x), with a remainder sss of lower degree than qqq (polynomial long division from school algebra, or the trick in the next example). Then

p(x)q(x)=mx+c+s(x)q(x),\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = mx + c + \frac{s(x)}{q(x)},q(x)p(x)​=mx+c+q(x)s(x)​,

and s(x)q(x)→0\dfrac{s(x)}{q(x)} \to 0q(x)s(x)​→0 as x→±∞x \to \pm\inftyx→±∞ by Theorem 3.10, so y=mx+cy = mx + cy=mx+c is an oblique asymptote at both ends.

Example 3.13An oblique asymptote✓ Checked

Find the asymptotes of f(x)=x2+1x−1,f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + 1}{x - 1}\mathclose{\text{,}}f(x)=x−1x2+1​, and decide on which side of each the graph lies.

Divide x2+1x^2 + 1x2+1 by x−1.x - 1\mathclose{\text{.}}x−1. Here a trick avoids long division: x2+1=(x2−1)+2=(x−1)(x+1)+2.x^2 + 1 = (x^2 - 1) + 2 = (x - 1)(x + 1) + 2\mathclose{\text{.}}x2+1=(x2−1)+2=(x−1)(x+1)+2. So, for x≠1,x \ne 1\mathclose{\text{,}}x=1,

As x→±∞,x \to \pm\infty\mathclose{\text{,}}x→±∞, 2x−1→0,\dfrac{2}{x - 1} \to 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x−12​→0, so y=x+1y = x + 1y=x+1 is an oblique asymptote at both ends. For x>1,x > 1\mathclose{\text{,}}x>1, 2x−1>0,\dfrac{2}{x - 1} > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}x−12​>0, so the graph lies above the asymptote; for x<1,x < 1\mathclose{\text{,}}x<1, it lies below. At x=1x = 1x=1 the numerator is 2≠02 \ne 02=0 and the denominator tends to 0, positive on the right and negative on the left, so by Theorem 3.9

lim⁡x→1+f(x)=∞,lim⁡x→1−f(x)=−∞,\lim_{x\to1^+} f(x) = \infty, \qquad \lim_{x\to1^-} f(x) = -\infty,x→1+lim​f(x)=∞,x→1−lim​f(x)=−∞,

and x=1x = 1x=1 is a vertical asymptote. There is no horizontal asymptote: f(x)→∞f(x) \to \inftyf(x)→∞ as x→∞x \to \inftyx→∞ and f(x)→−∞f(x) \to -\inftyf(x)→−∞ as x→−∞.x \to -\infty\mathclose{\text{.}}x→−∞. Figure 3.5 shows the graph and its asymptotes.

Compute itAsymptotes and continuity with SymPy

In SymPy, ∞\infty∞ is sp.oo. Here are the limits of Example 3.12 at both ends, and on both sides of 3:

Python
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x')
f = sp.sqrt(4*x**2 + 1)/(x - 3)
print(sp.limit(f, x, sp.oo), sp.limit(f, x, -sp.oo))
print(sp.limit(f, x, 3, '+'), sp.limit(f, x, 3, '-'))
Output
2 -2
oo -oo

As Module 2 warned, a one-sided limit needs its direction: without one, limit approaches from the right. To see where a function is continuous, continuous_domain lists the intervals; here is the function rrr of Example 3.2:

Python
from sympy.calculus.util import continuous_domain
r = (x**2 - 4)/(x**2 - x - 2)
print(continuous_domain(r, x, sp.S.Reals))
Output
Union(Interval.open(-oo, -1), Interval.open(-1, 2), Interval.open(2, oo))

Interval.open(-oo, -1) is the open interval (−∞,−1):(-\infty, -1)\mathclose{\text{:}}(−∞,−1): rrr is continuous everywhere except at −1-1−1 and 2. The answer does not say what kind of discontinuity each point is, and for complicated formulas continuous_domain can be wrong, so compare it with your own reasoning. For an oblique asymptote, sp.div divides one polynomial by another and returns the quotient and the remainder:

Python
q, s = sp.div(x**2 + 1, x - 1)                  # Example 3.13
print(q, s)
print(sp.limit((x**2 + 1)/(x - 1) - q, x, sp.oo))
Output
x + 1 2
0

The quotient x+1x + 1x+1 is the asymptote, and the last line confirms that the distance to it tends to 0.

Definition 3.9Orders of growth

Let fff and ggg be positive for all large x.x\mathclose{\text{.}}x. Then fff grows more slowly than ggg as x→∞,x \to \infty\mathclose{\text{,}}x→∞, written f≪gf \ll gf≪g and read “f is much smaller than g”, if

lim⁡x→∞f(x)g(x)=0.\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = 0.x→∞lim​g(x)f(x)​=0.

For functions defined at whole numbers n,n\mathclose{\text{,}}n, such as n!,n!\mathclose{\text{,}}n!, the limit as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞ means the same, with nnn running through 1,2,3,…;1, 2, 3, \dots\mathclose{\text{;}}1,2,3,…; Module 14 studies such limits of sequences.

So far out, fff is a negligible fraction of g:g\mathclose{\text{:}}g: eventually below 1%, or 0.0001%, or any fraction you name. Among powers, the higher power wins: xp≪xqx^p \ll x^qxp≪xq whenever p<q,p < q\mathclose{\text{,}}p<q, since xpxq=1xq−p→0.\dfrac{x^p}{x^q} = \dfrac{1}{x^{q-p}} \to 0\mathclose{\text{.}}xqxp​=xq−p1​→0.

Theorem 3.11Orders of growth

For every p>0p > 0p>0 and every a>1,a > 1\mathclose{\text{,}}a>1, as x→∞,x \to \infty\mathclose{\text{,}}x→∞,

ln⁡x≪xp≪ax,\ln x \ll x^p \ll a^x,lnx≪xp≪ax,

and, as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞ through the whole numbers,

an≪n!≪nn.a^n \ll n! \ll n^n.an≪n!≪nn.

Every logarithm loses to every positive power, every power to every exponential with base greater than 1, and every exponential to the factorial. The two comparisons with n!n!n! need only simple inequalities.

Big-O notation and algorithms

Computer scientists compare algorithms by how their running time grows with the size nnn of the input, such as the number of items to sort. Constant factors depend on the computer and the programmer, so the comparison ignores them.

Definition 3.10Big-O notation

Let fff and ggg be functions of a whole number n.n\mathclose{\text{.}}n. Then f(n)=O(g(n))f(n) = O\big(g(n)\big)f(n)=O(g(n)) as n→∞,n \to \infty\mathclose{\text{,}}n→∞, read “fff of nnn is big-O of ggg of nnn”, if there are constants CCC and NNN such that

∣f(n)∣≤C ∣g(n)∣for every n≥N.\abs{f(n)} \le C\,\abs{g(n)} \quad\text{for every } n \ge N.∣f(n)∣≤C∣g(n)∣for every n≥N.

So f=O(g)f = O(g)f=O(g) says that fff grows no faster than a constant multiple of g;g\mathclose{\text{;}}g; constant factors, and small n,n\mathclose{\text{,}}n, do not matter. It is only an upper bound: n=O(n2)n = O(n^2)n=O(n2) is true, if not informative. (The notation is also used as h→0:h \to 0\mathclose{\text{:}}h→0: Module 4 measures errors that way.) Limits give a quick test: if f(n)/g(n)f(n)/g(n)f(n)/g(n) tends to a number L,L\mathclose{\text{,}}L, then f=O(g),f = O(g)\mathclose{\text{,}}f=O(g), since eventually ∣f(n)/g(n)∣<∣L∣+1.\abs{f(n)/g(n)} < \abs{L} + 1\mathclose{\text{.}}∣f(n)/g(n)∣<∣L∣+1. In particular f≪gf \ll gf≪g implies f=O(g),f = O(g)\mathclose{\text{,}}f=O(g), but then ggg is not O(f),O(f)\mathclose{\text{,}}O(f), because g(n)/f(n)g(n)/f(n)g(n)/f(n) grows without bound.

For n≥1,n \ge 1\mathclose{\text{,}}n≥1, n≤n2n \le n^2n≤n2 and 1≤n2,1 \le n^2\mathclose{\text{,}}1≤n2, so

3n2+5n+7≤3n2+5n2+7n2=15n2.\begin{aligned} 3n^2 + 5n + 7 &\le 3n^2 + 5n^2 + 7n^2 \\ &= 15n^2. \end{aligned}3n2+5n+7​≤3n2+5n2+7n2=15n2.​

That is the definition, with C=15C = 15C=15 and N=1.N = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}N=1. The limit test gives the same: 3n2+5n+7n2=3+5n+7n2→3.\dfrac{3n^2 + 5n + 7}{n^2} = 3 + \dfrac5n + \dfrac{7}{n^2} \to 3\mathclose{\text{.}}n23n2+5n+7​=3+n5​+n27​→3. The lower-order terms 5n+75n + 75n+7 and the factor 3 do not matter.

On the other hand, n2n=n\dfrac{n^2}{n} = nnn2​=n grows without bound, so no constant CCC gives n2≤Cnn^2 \le Cnn2≤Cn for all large n:n\mathclose{\text{:}}n: n2n^2n2 is not O(n).O(n)\mathclose{\text{.}}O(n).

The common orders of growth in algorithm analysis, from the slowest-growing to the fastest:

Order Name Where it arises
O(log⁡2n)O(\log_2 n)O(log2​n) logarithmic binary search: halve a sorted list at each step
O(n)O(n)O(n) linear one look at each item, as in finding the largest
O(nlog⁡2n)O(n\log_2 n)O(nlog2​n) linearithmic sorting by merge sort
O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) quadratic comparing every pair of items
O(2n)O(2^n)O(2n) exponential trying every subset of the items
O(n!)O(n!)O(n!) factorial trying every order of the items

The base of a logarithm does not matter inside O:O\mathclose{\text{:}}O: log⁡2n=ln⁡nln⁡2\log_2 n = \dfrac{\ln n}{\ln 2}log2​n=ln2lnn​ is a constant multiple of ln⁡n,\ln n\mathclose{\text{,}}lnn, so computer scientists often write O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) without a base. Theorem 3.11 puts the orders of the table in a chain,

log⁡2n≪n≪nlog⁡2n≪n2≪2n≪n!,\log_2 n \ll n \ll n\log_2 n \ll n^2 \ll 2^n \ll n!,log2​n≪n≪nlog2​n≪n2≪2n≪n!,

since nnlog⁡2n=1log⁡2n→0\dfrac{n}{n\log_2 n} = \dfrac{1}{\log_2 n} \to 0nlog2​nn​=log2​n1​→0 and nlog⁡2nn2=log⁡2nn→0.\dfrac{n\log_2 n}{n^2} = \dfrac{\log_2 n}{n} \to 0\mathclose{\text{.}}n2nlog2​n​=nlog2​n​→0.

What this means in practice: suppose, hypothetically, that a computer performs 10910^9109 basic steps per second. For n=100,n = 100\mathclose{\text{,}}n=100, an algorithm that takes n2n^2n2 steps finishes in 10 microseconds; one that takes 2n2^n2n steps, about 1.27×1030,1.27 \times 10^{30}\mathclose{\text{,}}1.27×1030, needs about 4.0×10134.0 \times 10^{13}4.0×1013 years, and one that takes n!n!n! steps about 3×101413 \times 10^{141}3×10141 years. Faster hardware does not rescue an exponential algorithm: a computer twice as fast lets a 2n2^n2n algorithm handle only one more item in the same time, since 2n+1=2⋅2n,2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n\mathclose{\text{,}}2n+1=2⋅2n, while an n2n^2n2 algorithm handles 2≈1.41\sqrt2 \approx 1.412​≈1.41 times as many, since (2 n)2=2n2.(\sqrt2\,n)^2 = 2n^2\mathclose{\text{.}}(2​n)2=2n2.

Watch out

Big-O hides constant factors, and for small nnn they matter. An algorithm that takes 100 nlog⁡2n100\,n\log_2 n100nlog2​n steps beats one that takes n2n^2n2 steps only when n>100log⁡2n:n > 100\log_2 n\mathclose{\text{:}}n>100log2​n: for every nnn from 2 to 996 the “worse” quadratic algorithm takes fewer steps, and only from n=997n = 997n=997 on does the other win. Big-O says who wins in the end, not at the sizes you have. Measure as well.

Compute itGrowth rates with exact integers

Python’s whole numbers are exact, however large, so they can settle questions about growth without rounding errors. Where does 2n2^n2n overtake n10?n^{10}\mathclose{\text{?}}n10?

Python
n = 2
while n**10 >= 2**n:          # exact integer arithmetic: no rounding
    n += 1
print(n, n**10, 2**n)
Output
59 511116753300641401 576460752303423488

How long would the algorithms of the table take, at a hypothetical 10910^9109 steps per second?

Python
import math
speed = 10**9                         # steps per second (hypothetical)
year = 365.25 * 24 * 3600             # seconds in a year
for n in (20, 50, 100):
    for name, steps in (("n^2", n**2), ("2^n", 2**n), ("n!", math.factorial(n))):
        seconds = steps / speed
        print(f"n = {n:3}  {name:>3}: {seconds:9.3g} s = {seconds / year:9.3g} years")

What you learned

  • fff is continuous at aaa when lim⁡x→af(x)=f(a):\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)\mathclose{\text{:}}limx→a​f(x)=f(a): f(a)f(a)f(a) is defined, the limit exists, and the two are equal. One-sided continuity handles jumps and the ends of intervals.
  • A discontinuity is removable (the limit exists), a jump (the one-sided limits differ), infinite (the values grow without bound) or oscillating. Only a removable one can be repaired by changing one value.
  • Sums, products, quotients (where the denominator is not 0) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, and limits pass inside continuous functions: lim⁡f(g(x))=f(lim⁡g(x)).\lim f\big(g(x)\big) = f\big(\lim g(x)\big)\mathclose{\text{.}}limf(g(x))=f(limg(x)). Polynomials, rational functions, roots, exponentials, logarithms and the trigonometric functions are continuous on their domains.
  • The Intermediate Value Theorem: a function continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b] takes every value between f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b),f(b)\mathclose{\text{,}}f(b), so a change of sign brackets a root.
  • The bisection method halves the bracket at every step: after nnn steps its width is (b−a)/2n,(b - a)/2^n\mathclose{\text{,}}(b−a)/2n, and its midpoint is within (b−a)/2n+1(b - a)/2^{n+1}(b−a)/2n+1 of a root.
  • The Extreme Value Theorem: a function continuous on a closed interval [a,b][a, b][a,b] has a maximum and a minimum value there; on an open or unbounded interval, or with a discontinuity, it may not.
  • lim⁡x→af(x)=±∞\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = \pm\inftylimx→a​f(x)=±∞ describes values that grow without bound; then x=ax = ax=a is a vertical asymptote, typically where a non-zero numerator meets a zero denominator. ∞\infty∞ is not a number: ∞−∞\infty - \infty∞−∞ and ∞/∞\infty/\infty∞/∞ have no fixed value.
  • lim⁡x→±∞f(x)=L\lim_{x\to\pm\infty} f(x) = Llimx→±∞​f(x)=L gives the horizontal asymptote y=L.y = L\mathclose{\text{.}}y=L. Rational functions behave like the ratio of their leading terms; when the numerator’s degree exceeds the denominator’s by one, division gives an oblique asymptote.
  • ln⁡x≪xp≪ax\ln x \ll x^p \ll a^xlnx≪xp≪ax for p>0p > 0p>0 and a>1,a > 1\mathclose{\text{,}}a>1, and an≪n!≪nn.a^n \ll n! \ll n^n\mathclose{\text{.}}an≪n!≪nn. Big-O notation, f=O(g),f = O(g)\mathclose{\text{,}}f=O(g), bounds fff by a constant multiple of ggg and ranks algorithms by how their cost grows.

Exercise 3.11★★★The hiker’s theorem

A hiker leaves the bottom of a mountain path at 7:00 on Saturday and reaches the top at 15:00. On Sunday she leaves the top at 7:00 and walks down the same path, reaching the bottom at 15:00. Her speed varies on both days, and she stops to rest now and then. Prove that there is a time of day at which she is at exactly the same point of the path on both days.

Show solution✓ Checked

Measure her position by the distance along the path from the bottom, and let LLL be the length of the path. Let u(t)u(t)u(t) be her position at time ttt (in hours) on Saturday and d(t)d(t)d(t) her position at the same time on Sunday, for 7≤t≤15.7 \le t \le 15\mathclose{\text{.}}7≤t≤15. Both are continuous functions of t:t\mathclose{\text{:}}t: she cannot jump from one point of the path to another. So

g(t)=u(t)−d(t)g(t) = u(t) - d(t)g(t)=u(t)−d(t)

is continuous on [7,15][7, 15][7,15] (Theorem 3.1). At the start of the day g(7)=u(7)−d(7)=0−L=−L<0,g(7) = u(7) - d(7) = 0 - L = -L < 0\mathclose{\text{,}}g(7)=u(7)−d(7)=0−L=−L<0, and at the end g(15)=L−0=L>0.g(15) = L - 0 = L > 0\mathclose{\text{.}}g(15)=L−0=L>0. By the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a time ccc in (7,15)(7, 15)(7,15) with g(c)=0,g(c) = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}g(c)=0, that is, u(c)=d(c):u(c) = d(c)\mathclose{\text{:}}u(c)=d(c): at time ccc she is at the same point on both days.

The same argument as a picture: two hikers on one day, one walking up on Saturday’s schedule and one walking down on Sunday’s, must meet somewhere. s=5−12≈0.618,t=7+8s≈11.94.\begin{aligned} s &= \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2} \approx 0.618, \\ t &= 7 + 8s \approx 11.94. \end{aligned}st​=25​−1​≈0.618,=7+8s≈11.94.​

So at about 11:57 on both days she is at the same point, about 38% of the way up (s2≈0.382).s^2 \approx 0.382\mathclose{\text{).}}s2≈0.382).
